docs.title: Open Study Buddy
docs.text:
Title: Open Study Buddy

Target Audience: High school students (grades 9–12) as the primary audience, with content accessible to motivated junior high students, college undergraduates, coding clubs, hobbyists, and the teachers and mentors who run school maker programs.

Prerequisites: The Learning MicroPython and Physical Computing course (or equivalent experience). Students should already be able to flash MicroPython onto a Raspberry Pi Pico, use Thonny and the REPL, write loops, functions, and modules, read a push button with debouncing, and drive a display. The first chapter reviews these basics briefly, but it is a refresher, not a first introduction. Basic arithmetic and the idea of a sine wave are helpful; no prior signal-processing, networking, or artificial-intelligence experience is assumed.

docs.title: Course Overview
docs.text:
Open Study Buddy is a hands-on course for building a low-cost, fully open, personal AI agent device from parts that cost a few tens of dollars. The device combines a Raspberry Pi Pico 2 W microcontroller, a large round 360 × 360 color display (the same display used in the Chrono Smart Clock kit), an I2S speaker amplifier (MAX98357A) with a small high-quality speaker, an INMP441 I2S digital microphone, and three momentary push buttons (Mode, Up, Down). Students write every line of MicroPython that runs on it. By the end, they own a desk companion that listens, shows what it heard, speaks answers aloud, and tells them what is due and when the next test is.

The course follows the fast-growing trend of personal agents: always-on AI software that carries out multi-step work on a person's behalf, such as checking calendars, summarizing information, and coming back when it needs a decision. Most commercial personal agents are closed, run on a vendor's cloud computer, and bill a monthly subscription. Open Study Buddy takes the opposite approach. The device is totally open. Each person, class, or school sets up and configures the agent behind it, chooses where that agent runs, and decides which data it may touch. A school can connect its agent to the school calendar to announce events, upcoming tests, and project due dates, and can give its device its own school mascot (for example, a griffin) that appears on the round display.

The device is capable because several technologies meet on one inexpensive board. The Pico 2's dual cores and DSP-friendly instructions run a real-time FFT on live microphone audio, which supports volume meters, spectrum displays, and wake-word detection ("Hey Pico"). The Wi-Fi radio on the Pico 2 W connects the device to the agent software, and to MQTT, the lightweight publish/subscribe protocol at the core of many open home-automation and alert systems, so that a school can push "test tomorrow" alerts to every device. The large round display, speaker, and buttons give the agent a face, a voice, and a physical interface. That display carries a lot of information for a microcontroller: 360 × 360 is 129,600 pixels, or about 259 KB per frame at 16 bits per pixel, so pushing a full frame buffer to the screen on every update is far too slow for a responsive device. Students therefore learn to write directly to the display, one region at a time, redrawing only the part of the screen that changed (the time digits, a spectrum bar, a status icon) instead of the whole frame. The default listening mode is push-to-talk; an always-on wake-word mode is an advanced option that requires explicit approval from a parent, teacher, or school before it is enabled.

The book is also a gentle, step-by-step tutorial on getting the most out of MicroPython. Each chapter adds one idea on top of the previous chapter and ends with a working device feature. Students learn the techniques that make real embedded systems work: I2S audio, direct-memory-access style buffering, assembly-accelerated inner loops, non-blocking event loops, timers, and talking to a network service. Students also learn the responsibilities that come with a listening device: privacy, consent, data minimization, and the difference between a device that stays local and one that sends data away.

docs.title: Main Topics Covered
docs.text:
• Personal agents and the Open Study Buddy architecture — what a personal agent is, how commercial cloud agents differ from open, self-hosted agents, and how a Pico-based terminal (listen, display, speak) connects to the agent software behind it
  • MicroPython review for embedded systems — the REPL, Thonny, mpremote, modules and imports, the machine library, GPIO, interrupts, timers, memory limits, and garbage collection
  • The hardware kit — Raspberry Pi Pico 2 W, the 360 × 360 round color display and its controller, the INMP441 microphone, the MAX98357A amplifier and speaker, push buttons, breadboard wiring, and power
  • Round display graphics — SPI display drivers, color formats (RGB565), text and fonts, clock-face geometry, icons, animation, and displaying a school mascot image; why full-frame buffer updates are too slow on a 360 × 360 display, and how to use direct writes to set a drawing window and update only the changed region
  • Buttons and user-interface design — Mode, Up, and Down button schemes, debouncing, long press, menu navigation, and a state machine for device modes
  • Digital audio fundamentals — sound, sampling, sample rate, bit depth, Nyquist limit, the I2S bus (clock, word select, data), and reading and writing audio buffers with machine.I2S
  • Speaker output — generating tones, playing stored audio, volume control, amplifier shutdown, and avoiding the device hearing its own voice
  • Digital signal processing on the Pico 2 — windowing, the FFT, frequency bins, magnitude spectra, log-spaced band energies, spectrum displays, and measuring speed with the cycle counter
  • High-performance MicroPython — pure-Python versus @micropython.viper and assembly inner loops, array buffers passed by address, avoiding allocation in real-time code, and benchmarking against a real-time frame budget
  • Microphone calibration and push-to-talk — measuring the noise floor and speech level, signal-to-noise ratio, level gates, clipping, and recording an utterance on a button press
  • Wake-word detection — enrolling a phrase, feature extraction, template correlation, rolling windows, thresholds, false-accept and false-reject trade-offs, and the honest limits of template matching versus trained models
  • Networking and connecting to an agent — Wi-Fi, HTTP clients and JSON on the school LAN, a swappable "brain" behind one small request contract, push-to-talk audio sent in chunks to stay inside the Pico's memory, WebSocket streaming for always-on mode, authentication, handling network failure, and why plain HTTP is acceptable only on a trusted classroom network (with an introduction to HTTPS)
  • MQTT and push alerts — publish/subscribe versus request/response, brokers (running Mosquitto on a school Raspberry Pi), topics and topic naming per school and classroom, QoS levels, retained messages, last-will, umqtt on MicroPython, non-blocking check_msg inside the audio loop, authentication, keeping the broker off the public internet, and how MQTT connects the device to open home-automation dashboards such as Home Assistant
  • Configuring the school agent — a progression from a small rule-based buddy server (about 100 lines, no LLM), to the same server with speech-to-text, text-to-speech and one LLM call, to an optional open-source self-hosted agent behind the same contract; reading school events from a hand-edited JSON file, then an iCalendar (.ics) feed (parsed on the server, never on the Pico), using TEST: and DUE: title conventions for tests and project due dates, daily briefings, reminders, and per-school customization
  • School mascots and personalization — preparing mascot images for a round display, themes, voices, and wake-phrase choices
  • Privacy, safety, and responsible listening — consent, parent and school approval for always-on listening, local versus cloud processing, data retention, student-privacy law concepts, a hardware mute, and visible "listening" indicators
  • Testing, debugging, and system integration — probes and self-test programs, measuring frame overruns, logging, and combining the clock, audio, DSP, and agent features into one finished device

docs.title: Topics Not Covered
docs.text:
• Building or training large language models, neural-network keyword-spotting models, or speech-recognition models (the course uses template correlation for wake words and relies on a separate service for transcription)
  • Installation and administration details of any single commercial personal-agent product (the course treats commercial agents only as context)
  • Cloud server administration, container orchestration, and production-grade web hosting (running a single MQTT broker and buddy server on a school Raspberry Pi is covered; clustering and high availability are not)
  • Printed-circuit-board design, soldering, surface-mount assembly, and custom enclosure design (the kit uses a breadboard and plug-in wires)
  • The C/C++ Pico SDK, Arduino toolchain, and custom firmware builds (the course uses stock MicroPython only)
  • Advanced DSP theory such as filter design mathematics, wavelets, and the derivation of the FFT algorithm
  • Bluetooth audio, cellular connectivity, and battery power-management design
  • Legal advice on student-privacy regulations (the course explains concepts and tells students to consult their school's policies)

docs.title: Learning Outcomes
docs.text: After completing this course, students will be able to:

docs.title: Remember
docs.text:
Retrieving, recognizing, and recalling relevant knowledge from long-term memory.

  • Define personal agent, push-to-talk, wake word, sample rate, FFT, I2S, and noise floor
  • Name the five hardware parts of the Open Study Buddy kit and state the job of each
  • State the pixel count and approximate byte size of a full 360 × 360 RGB565 frame
  • Identify the Pico 2 W pins used for the display (SPI), the microphone (I2S RX), the amplifier (I2S TX), and the three buttons
  • Define publisher, subscriber, broker, topic, retained message, and QoS level in MQTT
  • Recall the three I2S signals (bit clock, word select, serial data) and what each carries
  • List the Mode, Up, and Down button roles used in each device mode
  • Recall the default wake phrase ("Hey Pico") and the steps needed to approve always-on listening
  • State the audio frame size and sample rate used by the kit and the time that one frame represents

docs.title: Understand
docs.text:
Constructing meaning from instructional messages, including oral, written, and graphic communication.

  • Explain how a personal agent differs from a chatbot and how an open, school-hosted agent differs from a vendor-hosted cloud agent
  • Describe the data flow from a spoken question, through the microphone and Pico, to the agent, and back to the speaker and display
  • Explain why a sampled signal needs a sample rate above twice its highest frequency (the Nyquist limit)
  • Explain what an FFT bin represents and calculate the frequency of a given bin from the sample rate and FFT size
  • Summarize why a real-time audio loop has a fixed time budget and what an overrun means
  • Explain why updating the whole 360 × 360 display for every change is too slow, and how writing directly to a defined region avoids the cost
  • Explain publish/subscribe messaging and how it differs from HTTP request/response, and why it suits alerts
  • Explain how template correlation detects a wake word and why mean-subtraction is needed
  • Describe why always-on listening raises privacy concerns that push-to-talk does not

docs.title: Apply
docs.text:
Carrying out or using a procedure in a given situation.

  • Wire the display, microphone, amplifier, speaker, and three buttons to a Pico 2 W and verify each part with a self-test program
  • Write MicroPython that draws text, a clock face, and a school mascot image on the round 360 × 360 display
  • Update the display with direct region writes (set a window, then stream only the changed pixels) for clock digits, spectrum bars, and status icons
  • Capture audio from the INMP441 with machine.I2S and compute its loudness in real time
  • Play tones and recorded audio through the MAX98357A amplifier and control the volume with buttons
  • Run the assembly-accelerated FFT on a live audio frame and draw a live spectrum on the display
  • Calibrate the microphone, enroll the phrase "Hey Pico," and tune the detection threshold
  • Connect the Pico 2 W to Wi-Fi and exchange JSON with a school-hosted buddy server over HTTP POST, then send push-to-talk audio to it in chunks
  • Subscribe the Pico to an MQTT topic with umqtt and show incoming alerts on the display without blocking the audio loop
  • Publish device status (online, last wake, volume) to an MQTT topic on a school broker
  • Configure the buddy server to read events from a JSON file and then an iCalendar (.ics) feed, and announce events whose titles start with TEST: or DUE: on the device

docs.title: Analyze
docs.text:
Breaking material into constituent parts and determining how the parts relate to one another and to an overall structure or purpose.

  • Break the device into subsystems (input, audio, DSP, display, network, agent) and trace how data moves between them
  • Diagnose a silent microphone, a distorted speaker, or a blank display by isolating wiring, configuration, and software causes
  • Measure and compare the time of a full-frame update with the time of region-only updates, and decide which regions of a screen layout should be redrawn independently
  • Compare pure-Python, viper, and assembly FFT implementations by measured cycles and decide which fit inside the frame budget
  • Analyze a spectrum to tell silence, steady noise, a tone, and speech apart
  • Examine wake-word score traces and distinguish false accepts from false rejects and their likely causes
  • Analyze where memory and CPU time go in a running program and find sources of garbage-collection pauses
  • Compare HTTP polling, MQTT, and WebSocket for delivering a "test tomorrow" alert and for streaming audio, in terms of latency, memory use, and complexity
  • Compare push-to-talk with always-on wake-word listening in terms of privacy, power use, reliability, and user experience

docs.title: Evaluate
docs.text:
Making judgments based on criteria and standards through checking and critiquing.

  • Judge whether a wake-word detector is good enough using measured false-accept and false-reject rates at several thresholds
  • Critique the limits of template correlation compared with a trained keyword-spotting model
  • Evaluate the privacy and safety risks of a classroom listening device and decide which safeguards are required before it is turned on
  • Choose MQTT QoS levels, retained messages, and last-will settings for classroom alerts and justify the choices
  • Evaluate the risk of exposing an MQTT broker or agent to the internet and decide which authentication and encryption are required
  • Assess the trade-offs of running the agent locally, on a school server, or in a vendor's cloud in terms of cost, control, latency, and data exposure
  • Evaluate the answers an agent gives about school events for accuracy, and decide when the device should ask for confirmation
  • Justify the design choices for the button scheme, display layout, and audio levels based on user testing with classmates

docs.title: Create
docs.text:
Putting elements together to form a coherent or functional whole; reorganizing elements into a new pattern or structure.

  • Design and build a complete Open Study Buddy device that combines the clock display, push-to-talk, speaker responses, and spectrum visualization
  • Create a personalized school edition with its own mascot, colors, wake phrase, and voice prompts
  • Design a screen layout divided into independently updated regions (time, mascot, spectrum, agent message, status bar) that keeps the display responsive while audio is processed
  • Build an alert pipeline in which a school server publishes upcoming tests and due dates to MQTT and several devices subscribe and display them
  • Write a state machine that moves the device between clock, listening, thinking, speaking, and settings modes
  • Design a configuration for a school agent that reports the next test, upcoming project due dates, and daily events from a school calendar
  • Connect the device to an open home-automation dashboard, such as Home Assistant, through MQTT
  • Develop a new DSP-based feature, such as a clap detector, a noise-level monitor for a classroom, or a tuner
  • Capstone project ideas: a homework-reminder buddy for a class, a study-timer buddy that listens for questions, a classroom noise-meter buddy, or a school-event announcer with a custom mascot
  • Produce a privacy and consent plan that a teacher or parent could review before a device is deployed

docs.title: Chapters
docs.text: This textbook is organized into 18 chapters covering 326 concepts.

docs.title: Chapter Overview
docs.text:
1. Personal Agents and the Open Study Buddy Architecture - Defines personal agents, contrasts commercial cloud agents with open school-hosted agents, and introduces the Open Study Buddy device, buddy server, and the swappable-brain progression from rules to LLMs.
  2. MicroPython Review for Embedded Systems - Refreshes the MicroPython skills used throughout the book: the REPL, modules, the machine library, GPIO, timers, interrupts, memory limits, and garbage collection on the Pico.
  3. Sound and Digital Audio Basics - Explains sound waves, frequency, amplitude, sampling, sample rate, bit depth, and the Nyquist limit, and introduces the time and frequency domains that later audio chapters build on.
  4. The Pico Kit Hardware and Wiring - Introduces the Raspberry Pi Pico 2 W, round display, INMP441 microphone, MAX98357A amplifier, speaker, and buttons, with breadboard wiring, power, and the pin assignment table for the kit.
  5. Display Basics: Pixels, Color, and Frame Size - Covers driving the 360 by 360 round display over SPI, RGB565 color, frame buffers, clock-face geometry, and why updating the whole frame on every change is too slow.
  6. Drawing Directly to Display Regions - Teaches direct region writes, drawing windows, and dirty regions, then uses them for text, icons, sprites, animation, image loading, and displaying a school mascot on the round display.
  7. Buttons, State Machines, and Device Modes - Builds Mode, Up, and Down button handling with debouncing, long press, menus, state machines, non-blocking event loops, and on-screen feedback for each device mode.
  8. I2S Audio: Recording and Playing Sound - Shows how the I2S bus, machine.I2S, audio buffers, and audio frames capture microphone sound and play tones and stored audio while staying inside a fixed frame time budget.
  9. Signal Processing and the FFT - Teaches the Fourier transform, the FFT, frequency bins, windowing, magnitude spectra, loudness, and band energies, and uses them to build volume meters and spectrum displays.
  10. High-Performance MicroPython - Makes MicroPython fast enough for real-time audio using typed arrays, viper code, inline assembly, allocation-free loops, cycle counting, and benchmarking against the frame budget.
  11. Microphone Calibration and Push-to-Talk - Measures the noise floor and speech level, sets level gates, and records an utterance on a button press, using voice activity detection to find where speech starts and stops.
  12. Wake-Word Detection - Builds an on-device wake-word detector from audio features, rolling windows, and template correlation, and examines thresholds, enrollment, false accepts, and false rejects honestly.
  13. Wi-Fi, HTTP, and Connecting to the Agent - Connects the Pico to the school network using Wi-Fi, IP addresses, JSON, HTTP POST, and the requests library so it can send a request to the buddy server and read the reply.
  14. Streaming Speech, Security, and Network Resilience - Covers sending speech to the agent in memory-safe chunks, speech-to-text and text-to-speech services, WebSockets, tokens, HTTPS, and handling timeouts, retries, and offline fallback.
  15. MQTT and Push Alerts - Introduces publish-subscribe messaging with brokers, topics, QoS levels, and retained messages, and receives school alerts with umqtt without blocking the real-time audio loop.
  16. Configuring the School Agent and Calendar - Connects the buddy to school events using JSON and iCalendar feeds, server-side parsing, TEST and DUE title conventions, daily briefings, reminders, and per-school personalization.
  17. Privacy, Safety, and Responsible Listening - Addresses consent, data minimization, retention, student-privacy concepts, threat models, a hardware mute switch, listening indicators, and the approval process for always-on listening.
  18. Testing, Integration, and Capstone Projects - Combines probes, self-tests, logging, and diagnostics to integrate the display, audio, DSP, and agent features into one finished device and several capstone projects.

docs.title: How to Use This Textbook
docs.text:
Work through the chapters in order. Each chapter builds on the ones before it, so the dependencies between concepts are always respected: sound and hardware come before the display and audio code, and the network, school-agent, and privacy chapters build on the working device. The first two chapters are a refresher, so students who already know the Raspberry Pi Pico and MicroPython can move through them quickly.

Note: Each chapter includes a list of concepts covered. Make sure to complete prerequisites before moving to advanced chapters.

docs.title: A Desk Companion You Build Yourself
docs.text:
Picture a small round screen on your desk. You press a button and ask, "When is my next test?" A moment later the device answers out loud and shows a countdown on its display. It costs a few tens of dollars, you wired it yourself, and you wrote every line of code that runs on it.

That device is the Open Study Buddy, and this book teaches you to build it one feature at a time. Before we touch any wires, we need a shared vocabulary. This chapter defines the words that the rest of the book uses (agent, terminal, server, brain) and shows how they fit together.

Hello, Builders! I'm Sage

I'm Sage, an owl who loves listening closely, and I'll be your guide through this book. Here is what I do, in the order you will usually meet me in a chapter:

  1. Welcome: I open a chapter and tell you what you will be able to build.
  2. Think: I mark a big idea that is worth a pause.
  3. Tip: I hand you a shortcut that saves time.
  4. Warn: I flag a common trap and show you the way out.
  5. Encourage: I cheer you on at a hard spot.
  6. Celebrate: I close a chapter by naming what you just learned.

If I'm not doing one of those six things, I'm not in the chapter. Let's listen closely!

By the end of this chapter, you will be able to name every part of the device, explain which parts run on the desk and which run on a school computer, and trace one spoken question all the way to a spoken answer.

docs.title: What Is a Personal Agent?
docs.text:
A personal agent is software that carries out multi-step work on one person's behalf. Three traits set it apart from other programs:

  • It works for you. It acts on your calendar, your homework, and your reminders, not on a generic task.
  • It takes several steps. One request can trigger a chain of actions, such as looking something up, deciding, and then sending an alert.
  • It comes back when it needs a decision. If an action affects you, the agent asks before it goes ahead.

To do those steps, an agent uses tools, which are small programs it is allowed to run, such as "read the school calendar" or "send an alert." We define tools carefully later in this chapter. For now, think of a tool as one thing the agent can do.

docs.title: A Worked Example: Getting Ready for Friday
docs.text:
Suppose Maya says, "Get me ready for Friday's test." A personal agent could handle that request in five steps:

  1. It reads the school calendar and finds an event titled "TEST: Biology" on Friday.
  2. It checks for other deadlines and finds "DUE: Lab report" on Thursday.
  3. It builds a short plan: finish the lab report Thursday, review notes Thursday night.
  4. It schedules a reminder for Thursday at 7 pm.
  5. It asks Maya, "Should I move your study session to 6 pm?" and waits for her answer before changing anything.

Notice that Maya made one request, the agent did the multi-step work, and the agent came back with a question before it changed Maya's schedule. Those are the three traits in action.

docs.title: Chatbot Versus Agent
docs.text:
A chatbot answers one message at a time. You type, it replies, and then it waits for your next message. It does not read your calendar, it does not set reminders, and it does not act when you are away. A chatbot's reply is the whole job, while for an agent the reply is often just the last step.

The table below summarizes the difference using the traits we just defined.

Question Chatbot Personal agent Who starts each piece of work? You, with every message You for the first request, then the agent on its own How many steps per request? One reply Several steps in a chain Does it use tools? Usually not Yes, such as calendar and alerts Does it act when you are away? No Yes, such as a morning reminder Does it ask before acting? Not needed, it only talks Yes, before actions that affect you

Many agents contain a chatbot-style language model inside, so the line can look blurry. The test is simple: if the software only produces a reply, it is a chatbot, and if it takes actions for you, it is acting as an agent.

The next activity lets you practice that test on ten described behaviors.

docs.title: Diagram: Chatbot or Agent Sorter
docs.text:
Chatbot or Agent Sorter

Type: microsim sim-id: chatbot-or-agent-sorter Library: p5.js Status: Specified Template: https://github.com/dmccreary/conversational-ai/tree/main/docs/sims/chat-interface-anatomy Bloom Level: Analyze Bloom Verb: distinguish Learning Objective: The learner will distinguish chatbot behaviors from personal-agent behaviors by classifying 10 described behaviors, with at least 8 of 10 correct on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: personal agent, chatbot, tool, multi-step work (all defined in the section "What Is a Personal Agent?" above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: For each of the 10 behaviors, the learner commits to one of two bins, "Chatbot behavior" or "Agent behavior". A classification is correct when it matches the Correct bin column in Content. Mastery is 8 of 10 correct. Reading a behavior without committing is not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) Any program that talks is an agent. (2) A chatbot that sounds smart is an agent. (3) An agent must be a robot or a physical device.

Instructional Rationale: Analyze-level distinguishing requires the learner to apply the three traits to new cases rather than recite them. A forced two-way choice on concrete behaviors makes the learner decide which trait is present, and the one-sentence reason after each answer names the trait.

Content:

The learner sees the behaviors one at a time in this fixed order:

# Behavior shown to the learner Correct bin Why (shown as feedback) 1 Answers one typed question, then waits for the next message. Chatbot behavior It replies to a single message and takes no further action. 2 Reads the school calendar, finds a test, and adds a reminder for the night before. Agent behavior It uses a tool and acts in several steps without being asked for each one. 3 Explains what a "TEST:" event is when asked, with no access to any calendar. Chatbot behavior It gives information only and takes no action for the person. 4 Asks "Should I move your study session to 6 pm?" before changing the schedule. Agent behavior It comes back for a decision before an action that affects the person. 5 Rewrites a paragraph that the student pastes in. Chatbot behavior One request produces one reply, and the work ends there. 6 Checks every morning for new due dates and announces them. Agent behavior It acts on its own over time on the person's behalf. 7 Tells a joke when asked. Chatbot behavior It produces a reply only. 8 Sends an alert to the student's desk device when a test is one day away. Agent behavior It takes an action through a tool, without being asked at that moment. 9 Remembers that the student prefers 7 pm reminders and schedules the next reminder for 7 pm. docs.title: Where an Agent Lives
docs.text: An agent is software, so it has to run on a computer somewhere. Where it runs decides who controls it, what it costs, and what happens to your data. This section defines the computing terms first and then compares the three places an agent can live.

docs.title: Edge Devices and Always-On Devices
docs.text:
An edge device is a small computer at the "edge" of the network, close to the person who uses it, instead of in a distant data center. Phones, smart speakers, and your Raspberry Pi Pico are all edge devices. Their strengths are speed and presence: a button press is handled right where you are.

The Pico has a catch. It has only about half a megabyte of working memory, thousands of times less than a typical phone. That is plenty for reading buttons and driving a display, but far too little to run a large AI model.

Worked example. When you press the volume button on your Study Buddy, the Pico changes the volume immediately, because that decision needs no network and no server. When you ask a question about your test schedule, the Pico cannot answer alone. It must pass the question to a bigger computer. Keep that split in mind, because it explains the whole architecture of this book.

An always-on device stays powered and ready to respond whenever you need it. Your desk Study Buddy is always on in this sense: it plugs into USB power and waits, so there is no boot time when you want an answer.

Two Phrases, Two Meanings

Watch out for mixing up "always-on" and "always-listening." Always-on means the device has power and is ready, while always-listening means its microphone is being processed all the time. This book's default is push-to-talk, and always-listening needs approval from a parent, teacher, or school first.

Worked example. Your Study Buddy sits on the desk all night, always on. Its microphone is not being processed until you switch it to listening. A different device with a wake word, such as "Hey Pico," would need to process sound continuously to hear it, which is why Chapters 12 and 17 treat that mode with extra care.

docs.title: Cloud Agents
docs.text:
A cloud agent is an agent that runs on a vendor's computers in a remote data center and that you reach over the Internet. The vendor owns the hardware, writes and updates the software, and usually charges a monthly subscription. Cloud agents are popular because they are easy to start: you sign up and begin.

The price of that ease is control. The vendor decides what the agent can do, what happens to the audio and text you send, and how long the service lasts.

Worked example. Suppose you ask a cloud agent about your test. Your question travels over the Internet to the vendor's data center and is processed there, under the vendor's rules about storage and use. If you stop paying, or the vendor changes the service, your agent changes or disappears. None of this is bad by itself, but you should know it is happening, and you cannot inspect or change the software.

docs.title: Self-Hosted Agents
docs.text:
A self-hosted agent is an agent that runs on a computer you or your organization controls, such as a laptop, a spare Raspberry Pi, or a school server. You choose the software, you decide which data it may touch, and you can read and change how it works. The price of control is responsibility: you keep it updated and secure.

Worked example. Alex's coding club runs a small agent on a spare Raspberry Pi in the lab. The hardware cost is paid once, the club decides what the agent can read, and members can change how it answers. The trade-off is time. When a software update arrives, someone in the club has to install it.

docs.title: School-Hosted Agents
docs.text:
A school-hosted agent is a self-hosted agent that a school runs for its students. One school computer runs the agent, and every student's device connects to it. The school configures it for school needs: which calendar it reads, what voice and mascot it uses, and how long it keeps any data.

Worked example. A school sets up one agent that reads the school calendar. Every classroom device asks that one server for the next event. When the calendar contains "TEST: Biology" for Friday, every device can announce it, and the school decides whether any request is saved or deleted. This is the setup the Open Study Buddy is designed for.

The Real Question: Who Controls It?

Notice that "cloud or not" matters less than "who controls it." Ask who can see your requests, who can change the agent's behavior, and who can switch it off.

docs.title: What "Open" Means Here
docs.text: The Open Study Buddy is open in two senses: its hardware and its software. These two ideas look similar but mean different things.

docs.title: Open Hardware
docs.text:
Open hardware is hardware whose design is published, so anyone can study it, build it, repair it, and change it. The kit is open in a practical way too: it uses common, documented parts that you can buy from many sellers, instead of a sealed box that only one company can service.

Worked example. Suppose your speaker cracks. Because the speaker connects through a standard amplifier board, you can unplug it and wire in another small speaker that suits that amplifier. You do not need the vendor's permission, a special part number, or a replacement for the whole device. Chapter 4 shows the wiring for each part.

The table below contrasts the two approaches.

Question Closed hardware Open hardware Can you see how it is built? No Yes, the design is published Can you replace a broken part? Often only with the maker's part Yes, with any compatible part Can you add a feature? Only if the maker allows it Yes, you can modify it Who can repair it? Usually the maker You, your club, or your school

docs.title: Open Source Software
docs.text:
Open source software is software whose source code is published under a license that lets you read it, run it, change it, and share it. MicroPython, the language you will use throughout this book, is open source, and so is the code you will write for the buddy server.

Worked example. Open the buddy server's rule file and find the line that says "Sorry, I only know about tests and due dates." If you want a friendlier message, you can change that sentence and restart the server. With closed software, the same change would mean filing a request and waiting.

Two cautions keep "open" honest. Open source does not mean free of work, because someone still has to maintain it. It also does not mean automatically safe, because anyone can publish code, including code with mistakes.

Read Before You Run

Before you run code someone else wrote, search it for network calls and see where it sends data. That one check tells you what leaves your device.

docs.title: The Open Study Buddy Device
docs.text:
Now we can describe the device itself. The Open Study Buddy device is a desk-sized hardware kit built around a Raspberry Pi Pico 2 W microcontroller, which is a small, low-cost computer on a single chip, with Wi-Fi built in. It has five groups of parts:

Part Its job on the desk Raspberry Pi Pico 2 W Runs your MicroPython program and connects to Wi-Fi Round color display (360 × 360 pixels) Shows the clock, the agent's words, and status INMP441 microphone Turns sound into digital numbers the Pico can read MAX98357A amplifier and a small speaker Turns digital audio numbers back into sound Mode, Up, and Down buttons Let you change modes, move through menus, and adjust values

Worked example. Here is a day in the life of one device. You press the Mode button to switch from the clock to listening, and ask your question. The display shows a "thinking" message while the answer is prepared, then the speaker reads the answer aloud. Afterward you press Up and Down to adjust the volume. Every step in that story uses one of the five groups of parts.

The whole kit costs a few tens of dollars, and Chapter 4 lists every part and its wiring.

docs.title: The Agent Terminal
docs.text:
The Pico cannot think like a large AI system, so the Study Buddy does not try to. It works as an agent terminal, a device that gives an agent ears, a voice, and a face, but not its brain. The terminal collects your input from the microphone and buttons, shows output on the display and speaker, and sends your requests to the computer where the agent actually runs.

An everyday comparison is a walkie-talkie. The walkie-talkie lets you speak and listen, but the helpful person you are talking to is in another room. Keeping the terminal "thin" has two benefits. It fits within the Pico's small memory, and you can upgrade the agent's brain without rewriting the device's code.

Worked example. When you ask for your next test, the terminal does three things: it captures your voice, it sends the request to the server, and it plays the reply it receives. It does not search the calendar or write the answer. If the school changes the calendar, nothing on the terminal needs to change.

docs.title: The Buddy Server
docs.text:
The buddy server is the program that receives the terminal's requests, decides on a reply, and sends it back. It runs on a nearby computer, such as a Raspberry Pi that the school keeps on its network. The buddy server holds the school's configuration, the calendar data, and the agent's decision logic.

One buddy server can serve many terminals at once.

Worked example. Three students in the same classroom ask for the next test at the same moment. Each device sends its own request with its own device name. The buddy server answers each request separately and sends each reply back to the device that asked, so three students hear three answers at the same time.

Ears and Voice Here, Brain There

Here is the big mental shift: the device on your desk is not where the thinking happens. It is the face, ears, and voice, and the brain can live in another room.

docs.title: How the Terminal and Server Talk
docs.text: The terminal and the buddy server are separate programs on separate computers, so they need an agreement about how to talk. That agreement has a name, and it makes the rest of the architecture possible.

docs.title: The Request-Reply Contract
docs.text:
The request-reply contract is the agreed format of what the terminal sends (the request) and what the server returns (the reply). The terminal does not need to know how the server decides its answer. It only needs to know what to send and what shape of reply to expect.

Before we look at an example, one definition: JSON is a plain-text format for labeled values, written as names and values inside curly braces. Chapter 13 teaches it properly. In the example below, the names device, kind, and text are illustrative, because the real contract is defined in Chapter 13. The request says which device is asking, what kind of request it is, and what the student said, already converted to text.

{
  "device": "desk-07",
  "kind": "question",
  "text": "when is my next test"
}

The reply says what to speak, what to show on the display, and which mode the device should go to next:

{
  "speak": "Your next test is Biology on Friday.",
  "show": "Biology test: Friday",
  "next_mode": "clock"
}

Worked example. Notice what the terminal does with this reply. It sends the speak text to the speaker, puts the show text on the display, and switches to the mode in next_mode. It never needed to know that the reply came from a calendar lookup. If a different server sent an identical reply shape, the terminal would work the same way.

docs.title: The Agent Data Flow
docs.text:
The agent data flow is the path one request takes from the student's voice to the spoken answer. Here are the eight steps, with the part that does each step in brackets. We use two new terms. Speech-to-text is a service that turns recorded speech into written words, and text-to-speech is a service that turns written words into speech. Chapter 14 shows how both are used.

  1. The student speaks. (Student)
  2. The microphone captures the sound as digital numbers. (Terminal)
  3. The request travels from the terminal to the server over Wi-Fi. (Network)
  4. The server converts the speech to text: "when is my next test". (Server)
  5. The brain decides on the reply: "Your next test is Biology on Friday." (Server)
  6. The server converts the reply to speech and packages the reply. (Server)
  7. The reply travels back to the terminal over Wi-Fi. (Network)
  8. The terminal shows the text on the display and plays the speech. (Terminal)

Step 1 is yours. Two steps happen on the terminal, three happen on the server, and two happen on the network between them. The word "brain" in step 5 means whatever logic decides the reply, and we examine it in the next section.

Check the Signal First

When your buddy stays silent, test the steps in order: microphone, Wi-Fi, server, then reply. Finding the first silent step is much faster than guessing.

docs.title: The Swappable Brain
docs.text:
Look again at step 5 of the data flow. Because the request-reply contract keeps the terminal separate from the decision logic, you can replace the logic without touching the terminal. That property is the swappable brain: the same device can talk to a very simple brain today and a much more capable brain next month.

A Lot of Words at Once

If eight new terms in a row feels like a lot, that is normal. You will build the simplest level first, and it uses only two of them: rules and tools. Come back to this section when each term shows up in code.

This section introduces the possible brains and the ideas around them, starting with the simplest.

docs.title: Rule-Based Agents
docs.text:
A rule-based agent decides using rules that a person wrote in advance, such as "if the question mentions a test, look up the next test event." It is small, predictable, and needs no AI model. It can run comfortably on a Raspberry Pi. Its weakness is that it only handles what its rules anticipated.

Before we look at code, here is what the example does. It lowercases the question text so that capital letters do not matter, checks for the word "test" or "due," and falls back to an apology otherwise. The helper next_event_with_prefix is illustrative, and Chapter 16 builds the real ones.

def decide(text, events):
    words = text.lower()
    if "test" in words:
        event = next_event_with_prefix(events, "TEST:")
        return f"Your next test is {event.title} on {event.day}."
    if "due" in words:
        event = next_event_with_prefix(events, "DUE:")
        return f"{event.title} is due on {event.day}."
    return "Sorry, I only know about tests and due dates."

Worked example. The question "When is my next test?" matches the first rule and gets a correct answer. The question "Do I have anything big coming up this week?" contains neither word, so the agent falls through to the apology, even though the answer is sitting in the calendar. That gap is exactly what the next kind of brain tries to close.

docs.title: LLM-Backed Agents
docs.text:
A large language model, or LLM, is an AI program trained on huge amounts of text that predicts and writes text. An LLM-backed agent uses an LLM to interpret questions phrased in many different ways and to write natural answers. The LLM does not run on the Pico, and usually not on a small buddy server either. It runs on a more powerful computer or a vendor's service.

Worked example. Ask the LLM-backed agent, "Do I have anything big coming up this week?" It can interpret "big" to mean tests and project deadlines, find "TEST: Biology" on Friday and "DUE: Lab report" on Thursday, and answer, "You have a lab report due Thursday and a Biology test on Friday." No rule was written for that phrasing.

The trade-offs are real. An LLM-backed agent needs more computing power. If the LLM is hosted by a vendor, your text leaves your school network. And an LLM can produce a confident answer that is wrong.

docs.title: Agent Tools
docs.text:
Agent tools are the functions an agent is allowed to call to fetch facts or take actions, such as "list upcoming events" or "send an alert." A rule-based agent calls a tool when a rule says to. An LLM-backed agent can choose which tool to call for a request it has never seen before.

Tools matter for two reasons. They give the agent real facts to work from, and they set limits, because the agent can only do what its tools allow.

Worked example. For "When is my next test?" the agent calls a tool named something like get_events with the filter "TEST:". The tool returns the real list from the school calendar, and the agent turns the first item into a sentence. The date came from the calendar, not from the model's imagination.

Confident Is Not Correct

An LLM can sound sure and still be wrong about a date. Make the agent read dates through a tool, and show the source on the display so you can check it.

docs.title: Agent Memory
docs.text: Agent memory is information an agent keeps between requests, such as your preferred reminder time or the topic of the last question. Short-term memory covers the current conversation, while long-term memory is stored and survives restarts. Memory is also data, so the privacy chapter treats it carefully.

docs.title: Agent Approval Rules
docs.text: Agent approval rules state which actions an agent may take on its own and which need a human "yes" first. For example: reading the calendar is allowed, sending a message to a classmate needs approval, and deleting an event is never allowed. These rules are how you apply the third trait of an agent, coming back for a decision.

docs.title: Open-Source Agent Frameworks
docs.text: An open-source agent framework is a published, reusable toolkit that supplies the common pieces of an agent, such as a loop that plans steps, tool calling, memory, and approval rules, so you do not write them from scratch. A school can self-host one and put it behind the same request-reply contract. This book treats frameworks as optional and does not teach a specific product, because the landscape changes quickly.

docs.title: Agent Progression Levels
docs.text:
Putting the pieces together gives a three-step ladder. The agent progression levels are the stages through which the buddy server grows, and each level keeps the same terminal and the same contract.

Level Brain What it adds 1 Rule-based buddy server (about 100 lines, no LLM) Fixed rules and tools that read the school calendar 2 The same server plus speech-to-text, text-to-speech, and one LLM call Spoken input and output, and free-form questions 3 An optional open-source agent framework behind the same contract Ready-made planning loop, memory, and approval rules

Worked example. Take the question "Do I have anything big coming up this week?" At Level 1 the server replies, "Sorry, I only know about tests and due dates." At Level 2 it replies, "You have a lab report due Thursday and a Biology test on Friday." At Level 3 it can add, "I can set a reminder for Thursday at 7 pm. Should I?" which uses the approval rules before it acts. The terminal code is identical at all three levels.

The last activity asks you to place abilities on the ladder.

docs.title: Diagram: Agent Progression Level Explorer
docs.text:
Agent Progression Level Explorer

Type: microsim sim-id: agent-progression-level-explorer Library: p5.js Status: Specified Template: https://github.com/dmccreary/ai-strategy-for-education/tree/main/docs/sims/ai-agent-anatomy Bloom Level: Analyze Bloom Verb: differentiate Learning Objective: The learner will differentiate the three agent progression levels by placing 8 abilities at the lowest level where each first appears, with at least 7 of 8 correct.

Prerequisites: rule-based agent, LLM-backed agent, agent tools, agent memory, agent approval rules, open-source agent framework, and the three levels (all defined in the section "The Swappable Brain" above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: For each of the 8 abilities, the learner commits to Level 1, Level 2, or Level 3. A placement is correct when it matches the Correct level column in Content. Mastery is 7 of 8 on the first attempt. Comparing the three replies in the second part is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) Only Level 3 can use tools. (2) A higher level needs a different terminal. (3) An LLM always gives a correct answer.

Instructional Rationale: Analyze-level differentiation requires the learner to tell which capability comes from which kind of brain. Placing each ability on the ladder after predicting, and then comparing the replies of all three levels to the same question, shows that the abilities differ while the request-reply contract stays the same.

Content:

The three levels are the values in the chapter table "Agent Progression Levels". The learner sees the abilities one at a time in this fixed order:

# Ability shown to the learner Correct level Why (shown as feedback) 1 Matches the question text against fixed rules a person wrote. Level 1 A rule-based server is made of exactly these rules. 2 Reads events from the school calendar using a tool. Level 1 Even the rule-based server calls tools when a rule says to. 3 Answers a question worded in a way no rule anticipated. Level 2 Interpreting free-form wording is what the LLM call adds. 4 Converts the student's speech to text and the reply back to speech. Level 2 Level 2 adds speech-to-text and text-to-speech. 5 Chooses for itself which tool to call for a new kind of request. Level 2 An LLM-backed agent can choose tools instead of following a rule. 6 Remembers a preferred reminder time between conversations using a ready-made memory feature. Level 3 A framework supplies memory so you do not build it yourself. 7 Asks for approval before a risky action using ready-made approval rules. Level 3 A framework supplies approval rules that apply before an action. 8 Runs a planning loop with tools, memory, and approvals supplied by a published toolkit. Level 3 That combination is what an open-source agent framework provides.

After the eight placements, the learner compares replies. The question is "Do I have anything big coming up this week?" and the learner chooses a level to see its reply:

Level Reply shown 1 "Sorry, I only know about tests and due dates." 2 "You have a lab report due Thursday and a Biology test on Friday." 3 "You have a lab report due Thursday and a Biology test on Friday. I can set a reminder for Thursday at 7 pm. Should I?"

For every level the sim also shows the same request and the same reply shape, with the fields device, kind, and text in the request and speak, show, and next_mode in the reply.

Provenance: The levels and the replies come from the chapter sections "Agent Progression Levels" and "The Swappable Brain". The calendar events are illustrative, and the sim labels them "illustrative".

Rules: A placement is correct when it equals the Correct level for that ability. The score is the number of correct placements, from 0 to 8. The request and reply fields are identical for all three levels. Only the reply text differs.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner reads ability 1 and chooses Level 1, 2, or 3.
  2. The sim shows whether it was correct and the Why text, then the learner continues through ability 8.
  3. After ability 8, the sim shows the score.
  4. The learner chooses a level and reads its reply to the sample question, and does the same for the other two levels.
  5. The learner should notice that the request and reply fields never change between levels.

Feedback: Eight abilities, fixed order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: ". Incorrect: "Not quite. This first appears at : ". The correct level is revealed immediately after each answer, and a running score "n of 8" is shown.

Starting State: Ability 1 is shown with the three levels, and the question "At which level does this ability first appear?"

Chapter Anchors: There are three levels. Level 1 is about 100 lines and uses no LLM. Level 2 adds speech-to-text, text-to-speech, and one LLM call. Level 3 is an optional open-source agent framework. The terminal and the request-reply contract do not change between levels.

docs.title: Putting It All Together
docs.text:
You now have the full picture. A personal agent is software that works for you in several steps and comes back for decisions. It can live in a vendor's cloud, on a computer you control, or on a school server. Your Open Study Buddy is a thin agent terminal, built from open hardware, that sends requests to a buddy server over a request-reply contract. The decision logic behind the server is a swappable brain that can grow from simple rules to an LLM to a full framework.

Key takeaways:

  • A chatbot replies, and an agent acts for you, uses tools, and asks before it changes something.
  • Cloud, self-hosted, and school-hosted agents differ mainly in who runs the computer and who decides what data it touches.
  • Open hardware and open source software let you study, repair, and change the whole system.
  • The Open Study Buddy device is an agent terminal with a Pico, a round display, a microphone, an amplifier with a speaker, and three buttons.
  • The buddy server receives requests, decides on a reply, and returns it, and one server can serve many terminals.
  • One spoken question travels through eight steps: one is yours, two happen on the terminal, three on the server, and two on the network.
  • Because of the request-reply contract, the brain can be swapped from rules to an LLM to a framework without changing the terminal.

Test yourself with these two questions, and click each one to reveal its answer.

A student asks a question worded in a way that no written rule anticipated. Which agent progression level first handles it? Click to expand

Level 2. An LLM-backed agent can interpret free-form wording, while a Level 1 rule-based server only handles questions that match its rules.

Which steps of the data flow does the terminal perform, and why does the server do the rest of the work? Click to expand

The terminal captures the sound (step 2) and later shows and plays the reply (step 8). The server does speech-to-text, the brain's decision, and text-to-speech (steps 4 to 6) because those jobs need far more memory than the Pico has, and the Wi-Fi link only carries the request and the reply (steps 3 and 7).

Vocabulary Unlocked

You just learned the vocabulary of a personal agent and traced one question from your voice to an answer on the display. From here on, when you read terminal, server, or brain, you will know exactly which job each one does.

In Chapter 2 we refresh the MicroPython skills you will use to program the terminal.

docs.title: Learning Graph for Open Study Buddy
docs.text:
Open Learning Graph Viewer Fullscreen

This section contains the learning graph for this textbook. A learning graph is a graph of concepts used in this textbook. Each concept is represented by a node in a network graph. Concepts are connected by directed edges that indicate what concepts each node depends on before that concept is understood by the student.

A learning graph is the foundational data structure for intelligent textbooks that can recommend learning paths. A learning graph is like a roadmap of concepts to help students arrive at their learning goals.

At the left of the learning graph are prerequisite or foundational concepts. They have no outbound edges. They only have inbound edges for other concepts that depend on understanding these foundational prerequisite concepts. At the far right we have the most advanced concepts in the course. To master these concepts you must understand all the concepts that they point to.

Here are other files used by the learning graph.

docs.title: Course Description
docs.text: We use the Course Description as the source document for the concepts that are included in this course. The course description uses the 2001 Bloom taxonomy to order learning objectives.

docs.title: List of Concepts
docs.text: We use generative AI to convert the course description into a Concept List. Each concept is in the form of a short Title Case label with most labels under 32 characters long.

docs.title: Concept Dependency List
docs.text: We next use generative AI to create a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG). DAGs do not have cycles where concepts depend on themselves. We provide the DAG in two formats. One is a CSV file and the other format is a JSON file that uses the vis-network JavaScript library format. The vis-network format uses nodes, edges and metadata elements with edges containing from and to properties. This makes it easy for you to view and edit the learning graph using an editor built with the vis-network tools.

docs.text:

docs.title: Concept Taxonomy
docs.text: The 326 concepts in the learning graph are grouped into 15 categories. Each concept belongs to exactly one category. The TaxonomyID is the 3-5 letter code used in learning-graph.csv. Categories are ordered from foundational material to the capstone projects.

docs.title: Personal Agents and Architecture (FND)
docs.text:
TaxonomyID: FND Concepts: 22

What a personal agent is, open versus cloud agents, the Open Study Buddy architecture, and the swappable-brain progression from a rule-based buddy server to open-source agent frameworks.

docs.title: MicroPython Review (MPY)
docs.text:
TaxonomyID: MPY Concepts: 20

The MicroPython skills the book assumes from the prerequisite course: REPL, modules, the machine library, interrupts, timers, memory limits and garbage collection.

docs.title: Pico Kit Hardware (HWK)
docs.text:
TaxonomyID: HWK Concepts: 22

The kit parts and their wiring: Pico 2 W, RP2350, round display, INMP441 microphone, MAX98357A amplifier, speaker, buttons and breadboard.

docs.title: Round Display Graphics (DISP)
docs.text:
TaxonomyID: DISP Concepts: 26

Driving the 360 x 360 round display over SPI: RGB565, frame size, why full-frame updates are too slow, direct region writes, clock faces, icons and the school mascot.

docs.title: Buttons and Device Modes (BTN)
docs.text:
TaxonomyID: BTN Concepts: 16

Mode, Up and Down buttons, debouncing, edge detection, menus, state machines, device modes and non-blocking event loops.

docs.title: Digital Audio and I2S (AUD)
docs.text:
TaxonomyID: AUD Concepts: 30

Sound, sampling, the Nyquist limit, the I2S bus, machine.I2S, audio buffers and frames, tone and stored-audio playback, and the self-hearing problem.

docs.title: Signal Processing and FFT (DSP)
docs.text:
TaxonomyID: DSP Concepts: 26

Time and frequency domains, the DFT and FFT, bins, windowing, magnitude spectra, band energies, loudness and spectrum displays.

docs.title: High-Performance MicroPython (PERF)
docs.text:
TaxonomyID: PERF Concepts: 20

Making MicroPython fast enough for real time: viper, inline assembly, the assembly FFT, typed arrays, allocation-free code, cycle counting and benchmarking.

docs.title: Mic Calibration and Push-to-Talk (CAL)
docs.text:
TaxonomyID: CAL Concepts: 14

Measuring the noise floor and speech level, signal-to-noise ratio, level gates, push-to-talk recording and utterance boundaries.

docs.title: Wake-Word Detection (WAKE)
docs.text:
TaxonomyID: WAKE Concepts: 24

Detecting 'Hey Pico': enrollment, feature extraction, template correlation, thresholds, false accepts and rejects, limits, and comparison with trained models.

docs.title: Networking and Agent Link (NET)
docs.text:
TaxonomyID: NET Concepts: 26

Wi-Fi, HTTP and JSON on the school LAN, chunked audio upload, speech services, WebSocket streaming, HTTPS, and handling network failure.

docs.title: MQTT and Push Alerts (MQTT)
docs.text:
TaxonomyID: MQTT Concepts: 22

Publish/subscribe messaging: brokers, topics, QoS, retained messages, last-will, umqtt, non-blocking check_msg, and connecting to Home Assistant.

docs.title: School Agent and Calendar (SCH)
docs.text:
TaxonomyID: SCH Concepts: 24

Connecting the agent to a school calendar via JSON then iCalendar feeds, test and due-date events, briefings, reminders and per-school customization.

docs.title: Privacy and Responsible Listening (PRIV)
docs.text:
TaxonomyID: PRIV Concepts: 18

Consent, parent and school approval, data minimization and retention, local versus cloud processing, threat models, mute and indicators.

docs.title: Testing, Integration and Capstones (TEST)
docs.text:
TaxonomyID: TEST Concepts: 16

Probe and self-test programs, wiring checks, logging, diagnosing silent microphones and blank displays, system integration and capstone projects.

docs.title: Pedagogical Flow
docs.text: The order above is the suggested teaching order. Personal-agent ideas, the MicroPython review and the hardware come first. Display, buttons and audio follow, then signal processing and performance. Calibration and wake-word detection build on audio and the FFT. Networking comes next, and MQTT builds on it. The school-agent, privacy and integration categories bring the pieces together.

docs.title: Gap Analysis
docs.text: 1. Main Topics (-1): 17 topics exceeds the 5-10 guideline. They are distinct enough to be useful for concept generation, so this is a minor point. Grouping them into four parts (Foundations, Audio and DSP, Wake word, Agent/alerts and responsibility) at chapter-design time will keep the book navigable.

docs.title: Improvement Suggestions
docs.text:
1. Speech-to-text and text-to-speech services. The description says transcription is a separate service and that Level 2 of the agent progression adds it. A one-line statement of which service (local or school-hosted) the labs use would sharpen the privacy outcomes.
  2. Wake-word status. The wake-word material is still unfinished in its source repository. Re-check the wake-word outcomes once those labs stabilize.
  3. Optional later extensions. Direct Google Calendar API (OAuth) and an open-source self-hosted agent (Level 3) are deliberately left as advanced extensions. Add outcomes for them only if they become labs.

docs.title: Concept Generation Readiness
docs.text:
Estimated potential concepts: 250-320.

  • Seventeen topics at roughly 12-18 concepts each gives about 200-300 concepts before de-duplication.
  • The audio, DSP, and wake-word topics are concept-dense (sampling, Nyquist, I2S signals, windowing, FFT bins, band energies, normalization, thresholds, false accept/reject).
  • The display topic adds performance concepts (RGB565 frame size, full-frame versus region writes, drawing windows).
  • The MQTT topic adds a separate cluster (broker, topic, QoS, retained message, last-will, check_msg).
  • Fifty-six outcomes across six Bloom levels suggest a healthy spread of factual, procedural, and evaluative concepts.

The description clears the 200-concept target.

docs.title: MicroSims
docs.text:
MicroSims are small, interactive educational simulations — each one focused on a single concept. They live under docs/sims/<sim-name>/ and are embedded into chapters via iframes.

New MicroSims can be created with the microsim-generator skill, which routes to the appropriate library (p5.js, Chart.js, vis-network, Mermaid, Leaflet, Plotly, Venn.js).

docs.title: Learning Graph Viewer
docs.text: This interactive viewer allows you to explore the learning graph for this course.

docs.title: Features
docs.text:
• Search: Type in the search box to find specific concepts
  • Category Filtering: Use checkboxes to show/hide concept categories
  • Interactive Navigation: Click and drag to explore, scroll to zoom
  • Statistics: View real-time counts of visible nodes and edges

docs.title: Using the Viewer
docs.text:
1. Search for Concepts: Start typing in the search box to find concepts. Click on a result to focus on that node.

  2. Filter by Category: Use the category checkboxes in the sidebar to show or hide groups of related concepts. Use "Check All" or "Uncheck All" for bulk operations.

  3. Navigate the Graph:

  4. Drag to pan around the graph
  5. Scroll to zoom in and out

  6. Click on a node to select it and highlight its connections

  7. View Statistics: The sidebar shows counts of visible nodes, edges, and foundational concepts.

docs.title: Graph Structure
docs.text:
• Foundational Concepts (left side): Prerequisites with no dependencies
  • Advanced Concepts (right side): Topics that build on multiple prerequisites
  • Edges: Arrows point from a concept to its prerequisites
